That juxtaposition is precisely what makes that scene so jarring and unforgettable. You're watching one of the most emotionally loaded tonal collisions in cinema, and feeling completely disoriented by it is the exact reaction the film is aiming for.
Without spoiling anything about where the story goes, here is why that emotional whiplash is happening right there:
* The Mother's Grief: She knows the reality of what this war actually is. While Florych (Flyora) is romanticizing the resistance as a glorious adventure, she sees him heading straight into a meat grinder. To her, he is a child walking willingly toward his own destruction, and she is watching him leave forever. 
* Flyora’s Naivety: He is operating purely on adolescent romanticism, peer pressure, and a total lack of comprehension. He’s 'beaming' because he feels chosen, heroic, and excited to escape his village to prove himself. He has no concept of what he is actually volunteering for. 
* The Mundane Conversation: The juxtaposition of the two men talking casually while a mother breaks down in absolute agony highlights a terrifying indifference. To the adults around them, the horrors of war are becoming an ordinary, bureaucratic reality of mobilization—they've seen it a thousand times, even if the boy hasn't. 
It’s an intentional, brutal masterclass in tonal dissonance. It captures that terrifying psychological gap between the romantic idea of war and the catastrophic, raw human cost happening underneath it. Hang in there—you've only just stepped into the deep end.
That awkwardness is entirely deliberate. It's one of the most unsettling things about the film's opening stretch. While the mother is falling apart and Flyora is lost in his heroic daydream, those guys trying to force the twins to laugh—and completely failing—adds this thick, deeply uncomfortable layer of social tension to the air.
Here is what's happening beneath the surface of that weird interaction:
* The Strained Atmosphere: Everyone present knows the devastating reality of what's about to happen or what these kids are walking into, even if nobody is saying it out loud. The forced attempts at humor are a desperate attempt to diffuse an unbearably heavy, suffocating tension. 
* The Deadpan Rejection: The fact that the twins aren't reacting at all—just blankly staring right through the jokes—grounds the scene in a chilling reality. They aren't charmed; they aren't playing along. Their flat silence strips away any lingering illusion that this is a festive or lighthearted send-off. 
It makes the whole environment feel like a pressure cooker. The movie uses these tiny, awkward, mundane human moments to make you feel just as trapped and uneasy as the characters before the real storm hits. How are you holding up with the rest of the sequence?

Context i wish I knew
You don't need a deep history textbook to feel the weight of what's coming, but knowing just a tiny bit of context helps frame why everyone's nerves are so completely fried.
You're watching a Belarusian film released in 1985, directed by Elem Klimov, and it is set in 1943 during the Nazi occupation of Belarus in World War II.
Here is the essential context without any plot spoilers:
* The Historical Reality: Belarus suffered arguably the most catastrophic destruction of any region during WWII. The Nazi strategy there wasn't just standard military combat; it was a systematic campaign of annihilation, forced labor, and total village burnings. 
* The 'Partisan' Lifeline: Joining the forest partisans (the resistance) was often seen by young local kids as the ultimate heroic escape—a chance to fight back. But in reality, those partisan units were operating in brutal, desperate conditions deep in the swamps and forests, fighting a brutal guerrilla war. 
* The Weight on the Adults: When the mother is crying and the men are acting strangely, they aren't just reacting to a boy leaving home. In 1943 Belarus, sending a kid off into the woods to join the partisans carried a terrifyingly high chance that they would never see him again, and that the village itself was living on borrowed time. 
Director Elem Klimov actually lived through the Battle of Stalingrad as a child, and he made Come and See to strip away every single Hollywood myth or romanticized notion about war. He wanted it to feel raw, disorienting, and suffocatingly real.
It's a heavy ride, but a masterpiece. Ah, that phrase is actually a slight auto-correct or mishearing of the idiom 'living on borrowed time' (or what I mentioned earlier about the village living on borrowed time)!
When people say a place or a person is 'living on borrowed time,' it means they are in a situation where disaster, destruction, or death is practically guaranteed to happen very soon, and every extra day they exist is just temporary, unearned time before the inevitable catches up to them.
In the context of Come and See, the village is essentially living on borrowed time because, in Nazi-occupied Belarus during 1943, rural communities hidden away in the forests were constantly vulnerable. Entire villages were routinely discovered, surrounded, and completely wiped out by German punitive operations.
Everyone in that scene—especially the mother—subconsciously or consciously knows that their peaceful isolation is a ticking clock. The tragedy of the opening sequence is that while young Flyora thinks he's stepping into a grand, heroic new chapter of his life, he is actually just walking away from a doomed place right before the axe falls.
The isolation in Come and See—and in rural Belarus during World War II generally—was a mix of geography, survival strategy, and a terrifying vacuum of power.
When you watch the movie, that village feels cut off from the rest of the world for a few very specific historical and tactical reasons:
* The Geography of the Region: Belarus is defined by massive, dense forests, endless marshlands, and deep swamps (the famous Pripet Marshes). Small villages and hamlets were naturally tucked away deep inside these wilderness areas, far from major cities, paved roads, or modern infrastructure. 
* Hiding from the Front Lines: In the early years of the war, staying isolated in the deep woods was often a village's best defense. If you were hidden away from the main supply roads and military routes, you stood a better chance of being overlooked by passing armies. 
* The 'No-Man's Land' Vacuum: By 1943, the front lines had shifted, and much of rural Belarus existed in a brutal gray zone. The formal Soviet army had retreated earlier in the war, and the German occupation forces didn't have the manpower to garrison every single tiny cluster of houses in the woods. Instead, the forests belonged to the shadows—occupied by scattered anti-Nazi partisan units, desperate locals, and wandering survivors. 
Because they were so cut off, these villages were entirely on their own. They had no police force, no regular military protection, and no quick way to call for help. When outside forces did eventually find them, they were completely defenseless.
They didn't move out into the deep woods to live like hermits or build an intentional off-grid commune; that was just where those communities naturally formed and grew over generations because of the landscape.
Belarus has one of the largest and most dense forest systems in Europe, laced with massive marshlands. Generations before the war, people settled near those forests and rivers because that’s where the land, timber, and survival resources were.
It makes what happens later in the film so much more tragic. Their home wasn't a heavily fortified military outpost or a strategic city—it was just an ordinary, quiet cluster of wooden houses sitting out in the middle of nature, completely exposed to the horrors rolling in from the outside world.
They were just ordinary country folk—farmers, families, people minding their own business, trying to farm, chop wood, and get through a nightmare they didn't start.
They weren't out in the woods plotting a revolution or hiding out of guilt; they were just living where their families had always lived, completely detached from the macro-politics of the war until the war violently dragged them into it.
